objective: Orpheus is a legendary Greek musician, poet, and prophet whose lyre playing can charm living creatures, stones, and underworld gods.；Eurydice is Orpheus' wife who dies from a snake bite.；Orpheus travels to the underworld to rescue Eurydice, charming guardians and gods with his lyre.

learningGoals.statement: Identify key characters and sequence of events in the Orpheus myth.
Explain the central themes of the Orpheus myth (trust, love, power of music, regret).
Compare two video versions of the Orpheus myth and identify core similarities and differences.

knowledgeNodes.name: Orpheus Myth Characters
knowledgeNodes.definition: Key characters in the Orpheus myth: Orpheus (legendary musician), Eurydice (his wife), Hades and Persephone (underworld rulers), Cerberus (three-headed dog).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Read a number of different types of literary, informational, and graphic texts designed or adapted for English language learners (e.g., folk tales from diverse cultures; letters; informational books and series; materials with graphs, tables, and charts; levelled readers; poetry)

knowledgeNodes.name: Orpheus Myth Plot
knowledgeNodes.definition: The sequence of events: Orpheus and Eurydice marry, Eurydice dies from snake bite, Orpheus goes to underworld, charms gods, gets permission to take her back, must not look back, looks back due to doubt, loses her forever, eventually dies and is reunited.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of a number of different types of adapted texts in a variety of ways (e.g., sequence events in a story; participate in teacher-led discussions about texts; retell content; complete a cloze passage; state the main idea of a short, adapted text containing familiar vocabulary and content)

knowledgeNodes.name: Orpheus Myth Theme
knowledgeNodes.definition: The central themes: trust and love, the power of music to transcend boundaries, the consequences of doubt and regret, and the value of second chances.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Respond to simplified or adapted texts in a variety of ways (e.g., explain why they like a particular book; participate in an informal class discussion about a text; compose an “in-role” diary based on a story character; explain how a text relates to their personal experience)

knowledgeNodes.name: Myth Version Comparison
knowledgeNodes.definition: Comparing two video versions of the Orpheus myth: both share the core plot (snake bite, underworld rescue, no-looking-back rule) but differ in focus on details (first version emphasizes post-separation and eternal reunion; second adds more character background and intermediate plot details).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of, interpret, and create a variety of media texts.

knowledgeNodes.name: AI Tool Usage Guidelines
knowledgeNodes.definition: Students may use AI for explaining difficult story segments, translating words, getting simple summaries, and looking up vocabulary definitions. They must re-read the original story after AI use. AI must not be used to answer homework questions or write assignments; students must use their own ideas.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answered incorrectly on diagnostic question diag-esldo-s6-0703-q1 about why Orpheus looked back.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Orpheus looked back out of curiosity or defiance, but the story says it was due to doubt.

miniLesson.explain: Orpheus looked back because he doubted that Hades would keep his promise. Hades had set a condition: Orpheus must not look back until both had left the underworld. But Orpheus was anxious and unsure, so he turned around too soon. This doubt caused him to lose Eurydice forever.
miniLesson.example: Imagine you are in a dark cave. Someone promises to lead you out, but says you must not look back until you see the sun. You start to doubt they are still there, so you turn around—and find they disappear. That's what happened to Orpheus.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Doubt destroys trust: Orpheus looked back because he doubted, not because he was curious.

guidedPractice.prompt: What feeling made Orpheus look back?
Explain in one sentence why Orpheus looked back at Eurydice.
guidedPractice.answer: He looked back because he doubted that Hades would keep his promise.

guidedPractice.prompt: How does Orpheus' doubt relate to the theme of trust in the myth?
guidedPractice.answer: Orpheus' lack of trust caused him to break the rule, leading to permanent loss, showing that trust is essential and doubt can have irreversible consequences.

reteachModules.trigger: What happened to Eurydice after Orpheus looked back?
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Some students think Eurydice was revived or saved later, but in the myth she was lost permanently.

miniLesson.explain: When Orpheus looked back at Eurydice before leaving the underworld, she was immediately taken back to the underworld permanently. This is because he broke the 'no-looking-back' rule given by Hades. Once he looked back, she was lost forever, and he could not bring her back again.
miniLesson.example: Orpheus doubts and looks back near the exit of the underworld, losing Eurydice permanently. She does not return to life.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Looking back means losing her forever. No second chance.

guidedPractice.prompt: What happened to Eurydice after Orpheus looked back?
guidedPractice.answer: She returned to the underworld permanently.
Because Orpheus broke the no-looking-back rule by looking back out of doubt.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does the story teach us about trust and consequences?
guidedPractice.answer: The story shows that doubt can lead to irreversible loss, and trust is essential even in difficult situations.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers incorrectly on diagnostic question about the power of Orpheus' lyre (e.g., thinks it only charms animals).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may underestimate the lyre's power, thinking it only charms animals, but it also charms stones and underworld gods.

miniLesson.explain: Orpheus' lyre has extraordinary power. Its music can charm not only living creatures like animals, but also inanimate objects like stones, and even the gods of the underworld, including Hades and Persephone. The lyre can calm storms and tame wild beasts. This power is central to the story, as Orpheus uses it to persuade Hades to release Eurydice.
miniLesson.example: In the myth, when Orpheus enters the underworld, he plays his lyre and charms the three-headed dog Cerberus, allowing him to pass. Later, he plays for Hades and Persephone, moving them to tears and convincing them to grant his wish for Eurydice's return.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think: The lyre can charm anything—from a tiny ant to a mighty god. It's like a magical remote control for all things.

guidedPractice.prompt: Name three things that Orpheus' lyre can charm.
guidedPractice.answer: Animals, stones, and underworld gods (Hades and Persephone).

guidedPractice.prompt: How did Orpheus use his lyre to get past Cerberus, the three-headed dog?
guidedPractice.answer: He played his lyre to charm Cerberus, making the dog calm and allowing him to enter the underworld.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why is the lyre's ability to charm the gods important to the plot?
guidedPractice.answer: Because it enables Orpheus to persuade Hades and Persephone to allow Eurydice to leave the underworld, setting up the crucial 'no-looking-back' rule and the story's tragic ending.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly answered the diagnostic question comparing the two video versions (diag-esldo-s6-0703-q4).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think the two video versions have different core plots, but they share the same core plot; differences are only in detail focus.

miniLesson.explain: Both video versions of the Orpheus myth share the exact same core plot: Orpheus marries Eurydice, she dies from a snake bite, Orpheus journeys to the underworld, charms Hades and Persephone, is told not to look back until they leave, looks back due to doubt, and loses Eurydice permanently. The differences are only in which details are emphasized. For example, one version focuses on the eternal reunion after death, while the other adds more background about the characters.
miniLesson.example: In the first video, the story emphasizes what happens after Orpheus loses Eurydice and their eventual reunion in the afterlife. In the second video, more time is spent on the characters' backgrounds and intermediate plot details. Yet both contain the marriage, snake bite, underworld journey, no-looking-back rule, and loss.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Same core story, just different details highlighted.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the core plot that both video versions share? List the main events in order.
guidedPractice.answer: Both versions share: Orpheus marries Eurydice -> Eurydice dies from a snake bite -> Orpheus goes to the underworld -> He charms Hades and Persephone with his lyre -> He is told not to look back until they leave -> He looks back due to doubt -> Eurydice is lost permanently.

guidedPractice.prompt: Give one specific detail that is different between the two video versions, based on the examples provided in class.
guidedPractice.answer: The first video emphasizes the eternal reunion between Orpheus and Eurydice after death, while the second video adds more background about the characters' lives before the snake bite.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate says, 'The two videos tell different stories.' Explain why this statement is inaccurate, using evidence from the class discussion.
guidedPractice.answer: The statement is inaccurate because both videos share the same core plot: marriage, snake bite, underworld journey, no-looking-back rule, and loss. The differences are only in which details are highlighted (e.g., one focuses on the afterlife reunion, the other on character background). The core story is the same.

options: She was revived and returned to life with Orpheus.
She was taken back to the underworld permanently.
She became a ghost that could visit Orpheus at night.

questions.stem: Explain why Orpheus's doubt led to the permanent loss of Eurydice. What rule did he break?
questions.rubric: Student must mention the 'no-looking-back' rule given by Hades, and that looking back caused Eurydice to be taken back to the underworld forever, with no second chance.

retestCards.passRule: For the single-choice question, the correct answer is B (index 1). For the open-ended question, the response must clearly state that Orpheus broke the no-looking-back rule and that Eurydice was lost permanently.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT something that Orpheus' lyre music can charm according to the myth?
options: Wild animals such as lions and wolves

questions.stem: Explain why the lyre's ability to charm the gods (Hades and Persephone) is crucial to the plot of the Orpheus myth.
questions.rubric: Student must state that Orpheus uses his music to persuade Hades and Persephone to allow Eurydice to return from the underworld, which sets up the 'no-looking-back' rule and leads to the tragic ending. Accept any clear explanation linking power to plot progression.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the answer must clearly connect the lyre's power to the underworld rulers and the story's outcome.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between the two video versions of the Orpheus myth shown in class?
options: They tell completely different stories with different main characters.
They share the same core plot but differ in which details are emphasized.
They are identical in every way, with no differences at all.
One version is correct and the other is a myth.

questions.stem: Name one specific difference in focus between the two video versions, based on what we discussed in class. Then explain why this difference does not change the core plot.
questions.rubric: Student must identify a valid difference (e.g., first video emphasizes eternal reunion after death, second adds more character background) and correctly state that the core plot (marriage, snake bite, underworld journey, no-looking-back rule, loss) remains the same. Accept any reasonable difference from the examples provided in class.

retestCards.passRule: Answer Q1 correctly (select option index 1) and answer Q2 with a valid difference and a clear explanation that the core plot is unchanged.
